summary: This work demonstrates quantum computational sensing (QCS) using a single superconducting transmon qubit with an integrated SQUID loop, where quantum signal processing interleaves sensing operations with trained control unitaries to encode task-relevant information into measurement outcomes prior to readout. For binary classification of static magnetic fields, the protocol achieves 3.0–14.9 percentage point accuracy improvements over Ramsey-based phase estimation, and for oscillating fields achieves 3.8–20.1 percentage points over dynamical decoupling, with advantages growing for more complex classification tasks.
motivation: Conventional quantum sensing first estimates a continuous signal parameter and then applies classical postprocessing to extract task-relevant information, discarding measurement information in the process. QCS instead directly encodes task-specific features into the measurement outcome, trading generality for efficiency by requiring less sensing time to complete a classification task.
method: A flux-tunable transmon qubit with $\partial f_{g-e}/\partial I_{\text{flux}} \approx 29$ MHz/mA sensitivity was biased away from the flux sweet spot to sense static ($0{-}5$ MHz detuning range, $T_s = 100$ µs) and oscillating (amplitude $0{-}5$ MHz or frequency $1{-}2$ MHz, $T_s = 200$ µs) magnetic fields through free evolution interleaved with trained X-rotations across $L = 2{-}28$ layers. Measurement outcomes were averaged over $S = 1{-}68$ shots and classified with random forests; protocols were optimized on a digital twin and benchmarked against optimized Ramsey and dynamical-decoupling baselines.
result: For static fields at 100 µs sensing time, QCS achieved 14.9 percentage point advantage over baseline on the most complex task and exceeded ideal shot-noise-limited baseline performance by up to 3.0 percentage points. For oscillating fields at 200 µs, amplitude and frequency classification improved by up to 20.1 and 15.4 percentage points respectively, with single-shot $T_1 = 30$ µs and $T_2^* = 8$ µs decoherence times and readout errors of $\sim 28$ % limiting performance.
